title: Necho II and the Phoenician circumnavigation of Africa
summary: Herodotus reports that the Egyptian king Necho II, after calling off a Nile to Red Sea canal, sent a Phoenician crew from the Red Sea to sail west around Libya (Africa) and return by the Strait of Gibraltar. They reportedly sowed and harvested grain each autumn on the coast and finished in the third year. Herodotus doubted their claim that the sun stood on their right. The account comes from Herodotus.

uncertainty.note: Herodotus gives no calendar date; Livius dates Necho II to 610-595 BCE, so the voyage lies within his reign. Years are astronomical (610 BCE = -609, 595 BCE = -594). The id year -600 is a midpoint, not a sourced date.

beats.caption: Herodotus says Necho sent Phoenician sailors from the Red Sea to sail around Libya and return through the Strait of Gibraltar.
Each autumn they came ashore, sowed grain, waited for harvest and sailed on; the trip took into a third year.
Herodotus credits Necho with first showing that Libya is surrounded by sea, though he disbelieved the sailors’ report of the sun on their right.

reviewer_note: Least sure: the voyage rests on Herodotus alone and he himself doubts one detail; confidence is set to contested. Dates come from Necho II’s reign, not the voyage. The Egypt point is a country centre, and the route around Africa is deliberately not pinned (Livius gives a modern reconstruction that I did not use). Bad Ancient is class other; Livius is a reference site.
